Most of the efforts in the HOST Surface Protection Subproject in FY 1986 were focused on thermal barrier coating (TBC) life prediction.
The TBC life prediction element is divided into contractual, grant, and in-house efforts.
The contracts with Pratt & Whitney Aircraft, General Electric Co., and Garrett Turbine Engine Co. are designed to produce 'engine-capable' TBC life-prediction models.
The grant with Cleveland State University is focused on finite-element modeling of TBC stress states.
The in-house work is focused on developing laboratory burner rig tests that can simulate the pressures and heat fluxes of aircraft gas-turbine engines.
The airfoil deposition modeling program element is concerned with modeling the deposition of corrodants onto turbine airfoils.
The chemically frozen boundary layer (CFBL) theory has been verified for segmented collectors simulating the turbine nose region.
The recently developed local thermochemical equilibrium (LTCE) theory agrees within 7% in predicting deposition rates compared to the CFBL theory.
Pratt & Whitney Aircraft has developed a preliminary TBC life model as part of the FY 1986 accomplishments.
Garrett Turbine Engine Co. has conducted an engine test as part of the FY 1986 accomplishments.
The rig development work includes modernizing the burner rig, adding computer data acquisition and limit monitoring, and implementing computer control.
The mechanical behavior of TBCs is being studied through a grant with Cleveland State University, with a focus on modeling the residual stresses.
The modeling strategy involves developing failure mechanisms models, mechanical behavior models, and a comprehensive life prediction model for the 'prime mode' design of components with TBCs.
The full benefits of TBCs can only be achieved when it becomes possible to use them in the 'prime-reliant' mode, where a failed TBC would lead directly to a failed component.
Advanced TBC life prediction models combined with other coating technology advances will be required before designers will be willing to use TBCs in the 'prime-reliant' mode.
